title: The AI Model Tier List
dek: A viral model tier list lands the same week that a misread FT chart, AT&T's open-model migration, and a flipped Vercel token graph all point the same direction: the question is no longer simply who has the best model, but how you assemble a stack that routes the right task to the right one — and NVIDIA, quietly, is buying its way into the open half of that future.

oneIdea.headline: The model war is no longer about who's best — it's about what belongs in your stack.
oneIdea.summary: Frontier models have crossed a threshold where they can all do a lot, and usage volume has exploded — so individuals, teams, and enterprises are shifting from 'which model leads' to model efficiency and complete model architectures that route the right task to the right model. Theo's tier list is the fun version of that conversation; AT&T serving 40% of employee queries with open models, routers cutting coding costs 56%, and open tokens flipping to 62% of Vercel's gateway are the serious one.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: Routing by task is already how a surgery thinks — it just isn't how the software is sold
items.body: The useful transferable idea from the tier list is not the ranking, it is the admission that different jobs want different tools. AT&T is reported to serve forty per cent of employee queries with open models and keep the expensive frontier ones for genuinely hard work, cutting coding costs by fifty-six per cent for a two per cent quality drop. General practice already reasons this way about people: the HCA does the blood pressure, the GP does the undifferentiated chest pain. The problem is that NHS primary care buys AI as single-product subscriptions, not as a stack, so there is no lever to route the cheap high-volume work — transcription, coding, letter drafting, inbox triage — differently from the small amount of work where you want the best available model and would happily pay for it. Worth asking any scribe vendor which model actually sits behind the product, whether it changes without notice, and what the quality-cost trade-off was that they chose on your behalf.

items.title: The Fable data-retention story is the real procurement lesson, not the pricing
items.body: The Financial Times chart was read as enterprises refusing to pay for the best model. NLW's counter is that the model carries a thirty-day data retention policy, and that alone is enough for a large number of organisations to refuse it outright. For a UK practice this is the whole conversation in miniature. Capability is not the binding constraint on what a surgery can adopt; data processing terms, retention periods, sub-processor lists and whether the DPIA survives contact with the ICB are. A tool two tiers down on somebody's ranking but with zero retention and UK hosting is the better clinical tool, because it is the one you are allowed to use on a real patient. When a vendor's demo is impressive, the next question is not how good the model is but where the audio and the transcript go, and for how long.

items.title: If Zitron's right / if NLW's right — the same defensive move either way
items.body: If NLW is right, the open tier keeps improving, routing becomes ordinary IT, and the cost of ambient documentation falls steadily — good news for a service that will never fund premium licences at scale. If Zitron is right, open models are the first stage of cost-cutting before abandonment, and his structural point bites: distillation needs something to distil from, so if frontier training spend collapses the cheap tier stops improving and then stops being maintained. For a Harrow practice the response is identical under both. Do not build a working week that only functions with one named product; make sure the clinical record holds the finished note in a form the practice owns rather than the vendor; and treat any price you are quoted now as an introductory one, because both men agree the current economics are being subsidised from somewhere. Buy on demonstrated workload relief this month, on terms you could exit in ninety days.

the_other_side.text: Zitron works from the same evidence and inverts all of it. He reads the AT&T migration not as a smarter stack but as the first move in cutting AI spend altogether — enterprises will save money "first by moving to open source models, then not using them at all", because in his view even open weights are expensive and of questionable use; he notes AT&T's headline 80-90% savings apply only to unspecified "certain applications" out of more than a thousand internal uses. He argues the whole debate about which model is cheapest misses the mechanism: "the problem is the amount of tokens that get burned", and labs are incentivised to build models that burn more of them. NVIDIA's Poolside deal, which the Brief reads as buying into the open-model future, he reads as vendor financing — NVIDIA "effectively becoming the GE Capital of AI", propping up customers who would otherwise fail. His sharpest structural point is one the Brief never addresses: "distillation requires a model to distill from", so a cheap open tier cannot outlive the frontier training spend it is supposedly replacing.

the_truth_beneath.text: The variable both men orbit is whether the cheap end of the model market is a durable architecture or a symptom of a subsidy. Both accept the same facts: frontier capability has bunched up, most work does not need the top model, enterprises are actively moving volume to open weights, and open inference is not free because a token costs compute whoever produced it. The empirical question that will resolve is what happens to that open tier when frontier training slows — the observable is whether new open-weight models keep matching last-generation frontier quality once labs cut training budgets, and whether routed enterprise workloads grow or get switched off entirely at renewal. The residue is pure worldview: Whittemore sees firms discovering efficiency; Zitron sees firms beginning to leave. Whittemore is vindicated if routed open-model stacks become standard IT and total useful workload keeps rising as prices fall; Zitron if the migration turns out to be the penultimate step before abandonment and the open tier degrades without frontier models to distil from. Both are polemicists with incentives — Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is where they agree despite opposite priors: neither disputes that most people do not need the frontier, and neither thinks open inference is actually cheap. Watch whether the next generation of open weights arrives on schedule, and at what quality.

headlines.headline: Hugging Face is shopping a $13B exit
headlines.summary: Business Insider reports Hugging Face has engaged an investment bank to field offers at a $13 billion price — nearly 3x its 2023 round at $4.5 billion, which included Google, Amazon, Nvidia, Intel, and Salesforce. No deal has been reached yet, but the platform now hosts more than two million models, 1.5 million datasets, and 1.5 million AI apps.

headlines.headline: Buying Hugging Face is a bet on permanent model fragmentation
headlines.summary: As open models multiply, the coordination layer — helping developers find a model, judge whether it's safe, and put it into production — becomes harder to replace. Both Stripe's purchase of OpenRouter and the interest in Hugging Face look like bets that model fragmentation is the future, with commentators immediately floating NVIDIA as the buyer that makes the most sense.

headlines.headline: NVIDIA pays $6B for Poolside's tech — and most of its engineers
headlines.summary: Per Eric Newcomer, NVIDIA struck a $6 billion non-exclusive licensing deal for Poolside's technology plus a $1 billion equity investment at a $12 billion valuation, hiring over 100 Poolside engineers — the bulk of the team — to work on Nemotron. Poolside insists 'this is not an acquisition and it is not an acqui-hire': the founders stay, aiming to keep AGI from being 'a closed technology controlled by a few.'

headlines.headline: Poolside's deal was born of a busted fundraise
headlines.summary: The founders told shareholders they had a six-week window at the end of last year to raise $2 billion for a 40,000 GB300 cluster coming online in January. They didn't close in time, lost the cluster, and realized they'd run out of compute and capital as soon as next year — making NVIDIA the partner of necessity for a frontier open coding model.

headlines.headline: NVIDIA is assembling the whole open-model stack
headlines.summary: Poolside for research talent, a stake in data-labeling startup Mercor (used for RL on the last two Nemotron models), and now a reported investment in Perplexity at a $30 billion valuation — a 50% markup — after initially floating a licensing-plus-hiring deal. Across all of these moves, NVIDIA is putting serious consideration into research, talent, training data, and the app layer as the open source frontier grows in importance.

headlines.headline: NVIDIA hikes chip prices 17% — on orders already placed
headlines.summary: The Information reports NVIDIA is notifying customers that top-end Grace Black and Vera Rubin chips will cost up to 17% more, applying even to chips ordered for delivery next year. A full 72-chip Vera Rubin rack is expected to hit $8 million, adding $5 billion to the cost of a gigawatt of compute — and cloud providers will 'almost certainly' pass it on. Blame the memory shortage, which looks set to stretch deep into next year or longer.

headlines.headline: Alibaba's record $10B share sale signals China's build-out is accelerating
headlines.summary: The largest offering of its kind in the Hong Kong market suggests China is pulling capital from every available source for AI — a departure from Alibaba's tight management of share supply. Michael Burry called Alibaba impressive as a disruptive force in the 'commodity low-cost LLM bloodbath,' but said he 'cannot bless share issuances' and expects return on invested capital to keep falling.

headlines.headline: Unitree's 460% IPO pop kicks off the humanoid hype cycle
headlines.summary: The robotics maker raised $900 million on the Shanghai Stock Exchange, debuted at a $9 billion market cap, and surged more than 460% on day one — a sign of strong appetite for China's embodied AI sector. Context matters, though: regulatory guardrails mechanically boost day-one performance, and this is the fourth Chinese IPO this year to rise more than 400% on debut.

headlines.headline: You sound like the person who would've been against the drum machine. It's a new tool for creativity.
headlines.attribution: Dr. Dre, in a New York Times profile
headlines.summary: In a New York Times profile, the rap legend said he's using AI extensively — a musical equivalent of brainstorming — and can't wait to see what happens next. Jimmy Iovine agreed ('when gifted people have AI, they're going to make better records') while noting AI companies have 'the worst public relations in the history of the world.' Both say plenty of producers are already using AI; they just won't admit it.

headlines.headline: Theo's tier list: Fable 5 alone at the top, Gemini in its own tier below F
headlines.summary: The AI entrepreneur and content creator put Fable 5 alone in S tier, GPT 5.6 Sol in A, and Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4 Flash, and GPT 5.6 Luna in B. Down in D: Anthropic's Opus 5 and Sonnet 5, GPT 5.6 Terra, and Composer 2.5. DeepSeek V4 Pro landed in F — and below F sat a dedicated 'Google tier' for Gemini 3.7 Flash and 3.1 Pro. Cue a ton of discussion.

headlines.headline: The real story is the diversification of model stacks
headlines.summary: The tier list matters not because it's fun to debate (though it is) but because individuals and increasingly businesses aren't picking one model — they're building infrastructure that moves between models by task. There's even a whole category of router companies built for exactly this, the best known of which, OpenRouter, was just acquired by Stripe for $7 billion.

headlines.headline: The 'businesses won't pay for Fable 5' chart misses the real reason
headlines.summary: The Financial Times chart showing limited enterprise spend on Fable 5 was read as businesses consciously rejecting the price. But Fable 5 carries a 30-day data retention policy — a provisional safeguard from when the model came back online after being shut down by the government — and that alone is enough for a huge number of enterprises to say absolutely not. Note how aggressively OpenAI has been pushing zero-data-retention for frontier models this past week.

headlines.headline: The Ramp data has a double selection bias — and a startup blind spot
headlines.summary: The chart comes from Ramp's token and spend management product, so it samples tech-forward companies whose users are predisposed to cost control — as Simon Smith put it, 'Fable simply isn't cost-effective for most tasks.' And the shock that enterprises haven't adopted a months-old model misses the glacial pace of enterprise IT: people are still using GPT 5.2 and other nine-month-old models because that's what their companies give them.

headlines.headline: AT&T plans to serve 70% of its AI queries with open models
headlines.summary: Per The Information, AT&T will hold OpenAI and Anthropic spending flat and slowly supplant it with open models — already serving 40% of employee queries across its ~100,000 staff, with a target of 60-70%. VP of Data Science Mark Austin says open models are as good or better than previous-generation frontier models, which were already up to the task; frontier models stay for advanced work like code generation.

headlines.headline: AT&T's router cut coding costs 56% — quality fell just 2%
headlines.summary: The company is using NVIDIA's Nemotron plus open models from Meta and Google, routed by task. Switching to open models also let AT&T host part of the service in its own data center stocked with NVIDIA and AMD chips — often cheaper than renting cloud compute. Chinese models aren't in the mix yet, but the risk analysis is underway.

headlines.headline: Fable 5 is a genius that needs to be tamed. 5.6 Sol is a slightly dumber robot that does exactly what you tell it.
headlines.attribution: Theo, AI entrepreneur and content creator, in his tier-list video
headlines.summary: Theo's paradox: Fable is the only S-tier model — 'it knows more than any model I've interacted with,' the one whose code he wants to merge and the one he trusts to double-check everything else — yet if forced to pick, he'd keep Sol, his default. 'Fable is that genius at the company that no one wants to work with, but no one wants to fire because they're the smartest person there.'

headlines.headline: NLW's workflow matches: run both, then commit
headlines.summary: On any given day, the host is jockeying between Fable 5 and GPT 5.6 Sol — for many tasks initiating in both, going back and forth a little, then deciding which one to hone in on. That usually, but not always, ends up being Fable.

headlines.headline: The 'weakest' GPT 5.6 outranks the balanced middle one
headlines.summary: Theo puts Luna — theoretically the least capable of the three GPT 5.6 models — two tiers above the middle Terra model. Luna is 'smart, fast, and good at a bunch of random stuff' and his most-called model by volume, for tasks like categorizing code and reading content (nothing irreversible). Terra? 'It makes sense on a pricing chart, but doesn't make sense in reality for me.'

headlines.headline: Expect a lot of models to fall into an uncanny middle
headlines.summary: As labs compete on deliberate performance-efficiency trade-offs rather than just the state of the art, many models will end up neither frontier enough to justify a premium nor efficient enough for high-volume tasks. And price intuitions can mislead: Theo notes Kimi K3, despite being open weight, actually costs slightly more than Sol on extra high, because Sol does more with fewer tokens.

headlines.headline: The backlash: 'they're all fantastic, bro'
headlines.summary: A vocal strand of the discourse is tired of model connoisseurship — comparing it to arguing over favorite colors or Pokémon — and even Theo concedes a tier list isn't the best way to compare models given the many axes: task capability, cost, token efficiency, speed. 'Whether you're using expensive best-in-class stuff like Fable or surprisingly cheap and effective stuff like DeepSeek V4 Flash, it's kind of hard to go wrong.'

headlines.headline: Open models flipped Vercel's gateway in two months
headlines.summary: Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch showed that closed-model tokens went from roughly 72% of AI gateway usage in late June to 38% two months later, with open models rising from 28% to 62%. The data skews toward developers, but for some it shows exactly where the winds are blowing.

headlines.headline: The likely end state: closed labs keep the value, open models take the tokens
headlines.summary: Investor Gavin Baker reads the Vercel data as open source taking share from OpenAI and Anthropic even as both accelerated in July — meaning total token demand grew even faster. His prediction: closed frontier tokens end up as 60-90% of economic value but only 15-25% of tokens. And since an open source token costs just as much compute to produce, nothing about open source inference is free — which is bullish for AI infrastructure.

headlines.headline: Or maybe it splits three ways: add the 'state-of-the-art specialist'
headlines.summary: MIT's Christian Catalini sees three spend categories: cheap generalists (commodity open weights), state-of-the-art generalists (closed-lab tokens), and in the middle, state-of-the-art specialists that combine open weights with enterprise proprietary context. It's the thesis behind Microsoft Foundry, which lets companies post-train on their own data atop MAI models — though how common that becomes across enterprises is genuinely debatable.

headlines.headline: 'What's the best model' is no longer the only question that matters
headlines.summary: Increasingly, the job is understanding where different models fit for different reasons — and even slow-moving, single-ecosystem enterprises should set up environments where small groups can test approaches and hunt for these new efficiencies. Whether the days of getting excited about state-of-the-art releases are over, we'll find out soon: chatter says Fable 5.1 is coming shortly, while OpenAI's Astra has slipped to September.
